newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss minister apologises for "blackmail" remark.
newsitem.headline: Swiss minister apologises for "blackmail" remark.

text.p: Swiss Economics Minister Jean-Pascal Delamuraz apologised on Wednesday for describing as "blackmail" demands that Switzerland quickly compensate Jews for their wartime suffering.

Bowing to international criticism, Delamuraz told reporters he had written to World Jewish Congress President Edgar Bronfman to say he was "very sorry that I offended your feelings as well as those of...the Jewish community at large.

"I assure you this was not my intention. The information on which I had based my statement regarding the fund was inaccurate," he added, referring to a Holocaust memorial fund under discussion between Berne and Jewish groups.
The Swiss government said Bronfman responded within hours, sending a fax dated January 14 acknowledging receipt of Delamuraz's apology and adding:
"I look forward to (the) return of constructive work together with the Swiss authorities and the Swiss banks, to resolve outstanding questions which will further our goals of truth and justice."

Delamuraz angered world Jewish groups and Israeli politicians last month by saying Jewish organisations were demanding 250 million Swiss francs ($180 million) from Berne as compensation for allegedly profiteering from World War Two.
In a newspaper interview at the end of his one-year rotating term in the Swiss presidency, Delamuraz had said the demand amounted to "extortion and blackmail".

World Jewish organisations denied proposing any sums for a Holocaust memorial fund in December talks with Swiss special ambassador Thomas Borer, whose report to the cabinet said Jewish groups had suggested 250 million to 300 million francs.
Delamuraz's spokesman Yves Seydoux said Borer's report on meetings with the WJC and others in Washington and New York was the basis for Delamuraz saying Jewish groups had raised the figure.
Delamuraz had previously refused to apologise for the remark, saying only that he regretted being misunderstood.
The remarks caused the World Jewish Congress and Israel's quasi-governmental Jewish Agency to put a possible boycott of Swiss banks on their agenda for a meeting on February 10.

Delamuraz had repeated Berne's stance that any compensation measures should wait for the findings of a nine-member historical panel named by the cabinet two weeks ago to investigate the Swiss financial role in World War Two.

Swiss banks have started their own joint probe with Jewish groups into allegations they hoarded dormant wealth of Holocaust victims and stonewalled family members who later sought the funds. ($1=1.3719 Swiss Franc)
